title: Bunk records, banjo lessons with Lawrence, sitting in with George Lewis
summary: Listened to Bunk's Columbia album, heard the Dukes of Dixieland guitarist, took up banjo and studied with Lawrence at home, then sat in with George Lewis at Manny's and met older musicians.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Let's see. Mostly Bunk. I can't think of anybody else offhand that I really listened to. I listened to Bunk and George and basically those people. Basically the album that Bunk put out, you know, when he went to New York, the Columbia album. And that was very interesting to me. What tunes were on that? High Society. I remember High Society and I remember Snagget. Snagget was on there. And that's all I can recall right now. But I used to listen to that album over and over again. It was very stimulating. And later on, we went to a Pops concert. This is when I was about eleven. And this is when the Dukes of Dixieland had first formed their little band. And they had a guitarist with them. And I got a big kick out of this. And I decided I wanted to start playing guitar. But in some way I got sidetracked to playing banjo. And then I learned that Lawrence was in town and I started taking from Lawrence. And the arrangement was that Lawrence would come up to the house. And of course we lived out in the suburbs in Lakeview. And this old colored fella would come up to the house, you know, and with the banjo. And people began to notice that there was something slightly different about our attitude towards life and family. And Lawrence was more or less part of the family and I was more or less part of his family. We'd always have some gumbo fun. My mother's a very good cook. And we'd sit around eating and then he'd... Mostly we'd sit around and play the blues, you know. Or we'd go through this little banjo method that he had. And we'd talk. I think that the talking part of it was the most educational. And later on I began sitting in with George Lewis. And I was about twelve then. When George was playing out at Manny's. Manny's Tavern. And I began making sessions around him. I began meeting the different older musicians. Amil Barnes and people I made those records with. Charlie, gee, I can't even remember his name. What did he play? A trumpet player. Charlie Love. Charlie Love. And it was a big kick meeting Albert Plenty. That's really something. And I began to do some, uh, do some, uh, reading on the history of jazz then. And, uh, read Rudy Blush's book. And became interested in the, you know, sociological aspects of it, in a sense. And, uh, are you interested in my complete development?
